pipeline.title: Start from zero
pipeline.outcome: Write and test a small Python program.

pipeline.title: Work like an engineer
pipeline.outcome: Put your program in Git and understand HTTP + JSON.

pipeline.title: Build the application shell
pipeline.outcome: Create a validated API and store its data. Take the data branch when your project needs it.

pipeline.title: Choose and use an AI model
pipeline.outcome: Build a small assistant with a pretrained model. ML and DL are deeper branches for training and understanding models; they are not gates for this route.

pipeline.title: Ground answers in your data
pipeline.outcome: Add document retrieval and citations when the application needs external knowledge.

pipeline.title: Measure quality before autonomy
pipeline.outcome: Test quality, privacy and hostile inputs. Add agents only when tools and multi-step workflows serve the problem.

pipeline.title: Deploy and operate
pipeline.outcome: Containerise the service, monitor failures and document rollback. Coding agents can help throughout the build.

domains.title: Python
domains.description: Write understandable, testable programs before adding models.

guide.goal: Write reliable Python programs before connecting AI tools.
guide.checkpoint: Build a JSON-based study tracker with functions, validation, logging and tests.
guide.bridge: You can now organise your code, collaborate in Git and understand HTTP requests.

domains.title: Engineering foundations
domains.description: Use the tools and contracts that make a team project maintainable.

guide.goal: Turn scripts into a maintainable, tested team repository.
guide.checkpoint: Open a pull request with a tested HTTP/JSON utility and reproducible setup instructions.
guide.bridge: Use these engineering habits while learning how data and mathematical operations work.

domains.title: Mathematics and data
domains.description: Understand the operations and data quality behind model behavior.

guide.goal: Understand the data, shapes, gradients and statistics behind AI.
guide.checkpoint: Clean a small dataset, plot its distributions and explain a dot product and gradient calculation.
guide.bridge: You are ready to serve validated data and predictions through an API.

domains.title: Backend and databases
domains.description: Expose reliable APIs and protect shared application state.

guide.goal: Build the API and database layer that an AI application needs.
guide.checkpoint: Build a FastAPI service with validated inputs, a SQL query and API tests.
guide.bridge: Next, learn what a predictive model does so you can compare and serve its results.

domains.title: Data Engineering + AI
domains.description: A distinct 10-phase roadmap: the data engineering backbone, AI/ML and LLM engineering, and a capstone for system design and interviews. It assumes SQL, Python, medallion warehousing, FastAPI and introductory Airflow are already familiar. Phases 1–7 build the DE backbone; Phases 8–9 can run alongside Phases 5–7 once the foundation is comfortable. Start Phase 10 after Phase 4 and keep it active throughout the rest of the roadmap. The two-year framing is a pace estimate, not a calendar schedule.

guide.goal: Extend the existing SQL, Python, medallion, FastAPI and introductory Airflow foundation into a production-oriented data and AI engineering sequence.
guide.checkpoint: Build and explain a reproducible CDC-to-lakehouse pipeline, then connect it to a measured ML or RAG workflow and a documented system design.
guide.bridge: This ten-phase roadmap is an optional parallel track. Phases 8–9 can overlap with Phases 5–7; begin Phase 10 after Phase 4 and keep practicing it throughout.

domains.title: Machine learning
domains.description: Train reliable baselines and understand what their evaluation actually measures.

guide.goal: Train and evaluate classical models without leakage.
guide.checkpoint: Compare a baseline and two models on a held-out test set; explain metrics and error cases.
guide.bridge: Use the same evaluation discipline when moving from classical models to neural networks.

domains.title: Deep learning
domains.description: Understand training mechanics, architectures and practical optimization.

guide.goal: Understand neural networks, backpropagation and practical optimisation.
guide.checkpoint: Train a small CPU PyTorch model; compare optimisers, save a checkpoint and explain tensor shapes.
guide.bridge: Attention and transformers prepare you to understand and use pretrained language models.

domains.title: LLM engineering
domains.description: Build grounded, bounded language-model features with a free local path.

guide.goal: Choose and use language models with deliberate prompts, context and outputs.
guide.checkpoint: Build a structured-output assistant with schema validation, recorded-response tests and a local-model option.
guide.bridge: Ground its answers in your own documents through retrieval and citations.

domains.title: Retrieval and RAG
domains.description: Connect answers to maintained evidence and evaluate retrieval independently.

guide.goal: Retrieve useful evidence and connect answers to traceable sources.
guide.checkpoint: Build a document search pipeline with chunking, hybrid retrieval, citations and retrieval measurements.
guide.bridge: Measure the complete system and test hostile inputs before giving it more autonomy.

domains.title: Evaluation and security
domains.description: Make quality, safety and failure behavior measurable.

guide.goal: Measure quality and protect the application against predictable failures.
guide.checkpoint: Create a golden dataset, regression report and prompt-injection tests with explicit failure handling.
guide.bridge: Use these checks and permission boundaries when adding tools, workflows and agents.

domains.title: Agents and MCP
domains.description: Build bounded tool workflows before increasing autonomy.

guide.goal: Build bounded tool workflows with state, recovery and human approval.
guide.checkpoint: Implement a tool workflow with an MCP connection, approval for sensitive actions and recovery tests.
guide.bridge: Deploy the tested workflow with containers, monitoring and reliable operations.

domains.title: Deployment and operations
domains.description: Release reproducible services and observe their real behavior.

guide.goal: Package and operate an AI service reliably within a small budget.
guide.checkpoint: Run the API in Docker Compose with health checks, timeouts, logs and a documented rollback.
guide.bridge: Use coding agents to maintain the service while keeping review and verification under your control.

domains.title: Coding agents
domains.description: Direct and verify generated work with clear engineering context.

guide.goal: Direct coding agents using clear specifications and verify their work.
guide.checkpoint: Write AGENTS.md and a task specification; review a generated change using tests and security checks.
guide.bridge: Connect these engineering capabilities to user needs, product decisions and documentation.

domains.title: Product and documentation
domains.description: Build useful products and document only what guides real decisions.

guide.goal: Deliver a useful AI product with evidence, feedback and maintainable documentation.
guide.checkpoint: Ship a small capstone with requirements, architecture, evaluation, deployment instructions and a runbook.
guide.bridge: Choose a team capstone, gather user feedback and revisit the lessons revealed by real failures.

lessons.why: Handle files and resources predictably when an AI pipeline stops halfway through an operation.
lessons.summary: Handle files and resources predictably when an AI pipeline stops halfway through an operation.

concepts.name: Context manager lifecycle
concepts.explanation: A with statement releases a resource when its block exits, including when an exception is raised.
concepts.example: Open a temporary text file inside with, raise an error and check that the handle closes.

concepts.name: Path resolution
concepts.explanation: Relative paths depend on the current working directory; use explicit project or data roots for repeatable execution.
concepts.example: Run a script from a different directory and demonstrate how Path(__file__) can locate a fixture.

concepts.name: Encoding and newline contracts
concepts.explanation: Text decoding needs an explicit encoding and a documented policy for malformed input.
concepts.example: Read a UTF-8 file containing Arabic and French text without losing characters.

concepts.name: Atomic replacement
concepts.explanation: Writing to a temporary file and replacing a destination on the same filesystem can avoid partially written outputs; atomicity is not the same as crash durability.
concepts.example: Simulate a failed JSON serialisation before replacement and verify the old destination remains readable.

concepts.name: Bounded input handling
concepts.explanation: Read limits and validation prevent an unexpectedly large or malformed file from exhausting memory or corrupting a dataset.

lessons.title: Async cancellation, timeouts and test doubles
lessons.why: Make concurrent network-style work predictable and testable without requiring a live paid API.
lessons.summary: Make concurrent network-style work predictable and testable without requiring a live paid API.

concepts.name: Coroutine versus blocking work
concepts.explanation: An async function can cooperate at await points but a blocking call still blocks the event loop.

concepts.name: Timeout boundaries
concepts.explanation: A timeout limits a particular operation; choose whether the budget includes retries and upstream waiting.

concepts.name: Cancellation cleanup
concepts.explanation: Cancellation is a control signal; cleanup belongs in finally and swallowed cancellation can keep unwanted work alive.

concepts.name: Bounded concurrency
concepts.explanation: A semaphore limits simultaneous work instead of creating an unbounded number of in-flight calls.
concepts.example: Run twenty fake requests with a concurrency limit of three and record peak active workers.

concepts.name: Dependency fakes
concepts.explanation: Replace an external dependency at a clear boundary to simulate successful, malformed and failing responses deterministically.

lessons.title: HTTP contracts, pagination and idempotency
lessons.why: Design predictable service calls so retries and changing datasets do not create inconsistent application behaviour.
lessons.summary: Design predictable service calls so retries and changing datasets do not create inconsistent application behaviour.

concepts.name: Safe and idempotent semantics
concepts.explanation: Safe methods are intended to retrieve without state changes; idempotent methods have the same intended effect when repeated.
concepts.example: Explain why repeating a GET should not create a new project and why a POST needs a separate deduplication contract.

concepts.name: Client versus server failures
concepts.explanation: Status codes describe classes of outcomes and should accompany a machine-readable error contract.
concepts.example: Return a validation error for an invalid page size rather than treating it as an internal server failure.

concepts.name: Pagination stability
concepts.explanation: Offset and cursor pagination have different behaviour as records change; a cursor needs an ordering contract.
concepts.example: Page a sorted list using a stable ID cursor and demonstrate how insertion affects offset pages.

concepts.name: Idempotency keys
concepts.explanation: A key associates repeated create attempts with one logical request; the server must check conflicting reuse and save the result coherently.
concepts.example: Replay a create request with one key and assert one record exists.

concepts.name: Contract compatibility
concepts.explanation: Adding optional fields is often easier to evolve than changing field meaning or removing a required response property.
concepts.example: Test an old client fixture against a response with one additional optional field.

lessons.title: Unit, integration and contract tests
lessons.why: Choose tests that catch boundary failures while keeping the feedback loop small and reliable.
lessons.summary: Choose tests that catch boundary failures while keeping the feedback loop small and reliable.

concepts.name: Unit boundaries
concepts.explanation: A unit test checks a small deterministic rule and avoids depending on live infrastructure.
concepts.example: Test a token-budget calculation with explicit fixtures instead of invoking a language model.

concepts.name: Integration boundaries
concepts.explanation: An integration test exercises real collaboration between components and can catch wiring or serialisation problems.
concepts.example: Send a request through a local API into a temporary SQLite database and verify the saved record.

concepts.name: Contract fixtures
concepts.explanation: A contract test protects assumptions about an interface independently of model-quality evaluation.
concepts.example: Validate recorded model responses against the same schema used in production.

concepts.name: Fixture isolation
concepts.explanation: Each test must receive controlled state so previous tests do not change its outcome.
concepts.example: Give each database test a fresh temporary directory and verify it does not read a developer database.

concepts.name: Failure-path assertions
concepts.explanation: A useful check verifies the intended error and state after failure, not only that some exception occurred.
concepts.example: Assert a timed-out create attempt leaves no half-written project and returns the documented error.

concepts.explanation: A derivative measures local sensitivity of an output to an input.

concepts.name: Chain rule
concepts.explanation: Derivatives of composed functions multiply through intermediate computations.
concepts.example: Differentiate squared prediction error through a linear prediction.

concepts.name: Gradients
concepts.explanation: A gradient collects partial derivatives for parameters; stepping against it locally reduces loss for a suitable step size.
concepts.example: Update w with w - learning_rate * gradient.

concepts.name: Distributions
concepts.explanation: Bernoulli describes binary events and normal distributions model continuous variation; assumptions should be checked.

concepts.name: Statistics

concepts.name: Vector norms
concepts.explanation: A norm measures vector size; normalisation requires handling the zero vector explicitly.

concepts.name: Projection geometry
concepts.explanation: Projecting one vector onto another measures its component in that direction and underlies many similarity calculations.
concepts.example: Project [2,2] onto the x axis and compare the remaining orthogonal component.

concepts.name: Eigenvector intuition
concepts.explanation: For a square matrix, an eigenvector keeps its direction under the transformation up to scaling.
concepts.example: Apply a diagonal matrix to its coordinate-axis vectors and identify the scale factors.

concepts.name: SVD and low rank
concepts.explanation: Singular value decomposition represents a matrix using orthogonal directions and singular values; truncation approximates it with fewer components.
concepts.example: Reconstruct a small matrix with one singular component and measure the remaining error.

concepts.name: Numerical conditioning
concepts.explanation: Nearly dependent inputs can amplify numerical error; solving a system is preferable to explicitly forming an inverse when possible.

concepts.explanation: The unit being sampled may be a person, document or time period rather than one row; uncertainty depends on that independence assumption.

concepts.name: Bootstrap intervals

lessons.title: Phase 1 · Distributed processing with Spark
lessons.why: Move from single-machine transformations to distributed processing, and learn to explain Spark plans, shuffles, skew and performance rather than treating Spark as a black box.
lessons.summary: Move from single-machine transformations to distributed processing, and learn to explain Spark plans, shuffles, skew and performance rather than treating Spark as a black box.

concepts.name: Spark architecture and execution
concepts.explanation: The driver builds a plan, executors run tasks, and a cluster manager allocates resources; jobs contain stages, which contain tasks mapped from a DAG. Lazy transformations are evaluated by actions. Catalyst optimizes plans and Tungsten improves execution; use explain() to inspect logical and physical plans.
concepts.example: Trace a filter, join and aggregation from a DataFrame action to its jobs, stages and tasks in the Spark UI.

concepts.name: Core APIs
concepts.explanation: RDDs explain Spark's distributed collection model; DataFrames provide schema-aware select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, agg and orderBy; Spark SQL runs through temporary views. Know that typed Datasets are mainly a Scala/Java API concern in a PySpark workflow.
concepts.example: Create a DataFrame, register it as a temporary view, run the same aggregation in SQL and DataFrame syntax, and compare the results.

concepts.name: Partitions, shuffles and skew
concepts.explanation: Partitions distribute work and default counts depend on input and configuration. repartition() redistributes data; coalesce() can reduce partitions with less movement. Grouping, joins, distinct, ordering and repartitioning can trigger shuffles, with map/reduce stages and disk spill. Detect skew through task-duration spread; mitigate with salting, broadcast joins or a suitable partition strategy.
concepts.example: Use a deliberately skewed key, inspect task durations, then compare a salted aggregation with the unsalted result.

concepts.name: Join planning
concepts.explanation: Broadcast hash joins, shuffle sort-merge joins and shuffle hash joins trade memory for network and sorting work. Spark can broadcast below its size threshold or use a broadcast hint; join reordering and predicate pushdown can reduce work. Skewed keys may need their own strategy.
concepts.example: Compare explain() plans for a small-dimension broadcast join and a large-large join, then push a selective filter before the join.

concepts.name: Memory, caching and spill
concepts.explanation: MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK and DISK_ONLY have different recomputation and storage costs; serialized and deserialized storage trade CPU for memory. cache() uses a default persistence level; persist() selects one explicitly. Understand executor execution/storage memory and unpersist materialized data when it is no longer needed.
concepts.example: Persist a reused DataFrame, inspect storage in the Spark UI, and unpersist it after the last dependent action.

concepts.name: Performance diagnosis
concepts.explanation: Use Jobs, Stages, Storage and Executors in the Spark UI to find long stages, skewed tasks, excess shuffles and GC pressure. Adaptive Query Execution can coalesce partitions and handle some skew. Parquet column pruning and predicate pushdown reduce I/O when queries select few columns or rows.
concepts.example: Capture a baseline and an optimized run, explain the changed plan and report task-time and input-size differences.

concepts.name: UDFs
concepts.explanation: Python UDFs pay row-by-row serialization and Py4J costs; Pandas UDFs use Arrow-backed vectorization and can help for operations unavailable in Spark's built-ins. Built-in Spark SQL functions are generally preferable because Spark can optimize them.
concepts.example: Implement one normalization with a built-in expression and a Pandas UDF, compare output equality and execution plans, and avoid a Python UDF when a built-in exists.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.explanation: Window.partitionBy() and orderBy() define per-group ordered calculations. row_number, rank and dense_rank differ on ties; lag and lead access neighboring rows, while window frames support running totals and moving averages.
concepts.example: Compute each customer's latest event, a tied rank, a running total and a three-row moving average; test tie and boundary cases.

concepts.name: Structured Streaming introduction
concepts.explanation: A streaming DataFrame shares the batch DataFrame API but executes incrementally, commonly in micro-batches. Watermarks bound state while allowing late events; append, update and complete output modes have different result semantics.
concepts.example: Run a small local event stream with a late record and compare watermark and output-mode behavior with an equivalent batch aggregation.

concepts.name: Deployment and I/O
concepts.explanation: Local, standalone and cluster execution differ in resource placement; client and cluster deploy modes place the driver differently. spark-submit exposes the main job configuration. Read and write Parquet, CSV, JDBC and cloud-storage paths with explicit schemas and safe credentials.
concepts.example: Package a parameterized PySpark job, run it with spark-submit in local mode and round-trip a small dataset through Parquet and CSV.

concepts.name: Debugging and observability
concepts.explanation: Executor failures differ from driver failures; common causes include out-of-memory errors, serialization errors and schema mismatches. Combine stack traces, explain(), getNumPartitions() and the Spark UI to diagnose instead of guessing.
concepts.example: Inject a schema mismatch and a partition imbalance into a local job, record the evidence from the error, plan and UI, and document the fix.

lessons.title: Phase 2 · Orchestration mastery with Airflow
lessons.why: Go beyond introductory DAGs to design, test, operate and debug reliable workflows that coordinate data systems without hiding business logic in orchestration code.
lessons.summary: Go beyond introductory DAGs to design, test, operate and debug reliable workflows that coordinate data systems without hiding business logic in orchestration code.

concepts.name: Airflow architecture
concepts.explanation: The Scheduler parses DAG files and decides what is ready; the Webserver presents the UI; an Executor dispatches work; the Metadata DB stores state; and the Triggerer handles deferrable work. Sequential, Local, Celery and Kubernetes executors trade simplicity for parallel and distributed capacity. Know where DAG files are discovered and how parsing works.
concepts.example: Trace one scheduled task from DAG parsing through scheduler state, executor dispatch and metadata updates.

concepts.name: DAG configuration
concepts.explanation: DAG schedule, start_date, catchup and max_active_runs determine when runs are created and how much work may overlap. Task dependencies can use >>, <<, set_upstream and set_downstream; pools, priority_weight and task concurrency limit contention.
concepts.example: Configure a daily DAG with a historical start date, disable catchup, cap active runs and show which logical dates are scheduled.

concepts.name: TaskFlow, XCom and branching
concepts.explanation: TaskFlow uses @dag and @task and is the preferred style for new Python DAGs; classic operators remain useful. XCom passes small metadata, not large datasets. BranchPythonOperator or @task.branch chooses paths, while trigger rules such as all_success, all_failed, one_success and none_failed control downstream execution.
concepts.example: Build a TaskFlow DAG that branches on a data-quality result, passes only a partition identifier by XCom and joins paths with an explicit trigger rule.

concepts.name: Dynamic task mapping
concepts.explanation: expand() and partial() create mapped tasks at run time from a collection; a static loop creates tasks during DAG definition. Map over a bounded list of tables, files or partitions, and understand limits on mapped task counts.
concepts.example: Map a validation task over a run-time list of table names and contrast it with a small static DAG.

concepts.name: Custom components
concepts.explanation: Custom Operators subclass BaseOperator; Hooks wrap external connections; Sensors wait using poke or reschedule mode with a poke interval and timeout. Prefer maintained provider components when they satisfy the use case; avoid building custom abstractions without a concrete need.
concepts.example: Write a small testable Hook and Operator around a local fixture, then explain why a provider is or is not preferable.

concepts.name: Reliability and production
concepts.explanation: Retries, retry_delay and exponential backoff recover transient failures; timeouts bound work. SLA settings and callbacks communicate missed expectations. Tasks should be idempotent so retries and backfills do not duplicate or corrupt data. Catchup and CLI backfills need safe ranges; success/failure callbacks can notify Slack or email.
concepts.example: Run a task twice against the same partition, prove idempotency, simulate a transient failure and document a bounded backfill and alert.

concepts.name: DAG design patterns
concepts.explanation: Avoid database/network work at module import time. Choose task granularity that balances observability and overhead. Prefer reschedule or deferrable Sensors over wasteful polling. Coordinate DAGs using TriggerDagRunOperator, ExternalTaskSensor or Datasets when the dependency requires it.
concepts.example: Use a Dataset update to trigger a downstream DAG and verify importing the DAG does not execute its workload.

concepts.name: Integrations
concepts.explanation: Airflow can run dbt through a BashOperator, Cosmos or a dbt Cloud provider; Spark through SparkSubmitOperator or an API/Livy; and connect through Postgres, S3/GCS, Kafka and HTTP providers. Pick integration boundaries that keep the data work testable.
concepts.example: Orchestrate a local transformation and a Spark job with explicit upstream/downstream contracts and no credentials in source.

concepts.name: Deployment and configuration
concepts.explanation: Run Airflow locally with Docker Compose; understand KubernetesExecutor tasks as pods and set task resource requests/limits. Know essential airflow.cfg settings, Connections and Variables, and use a secrets backend such as Vault or a cloud secrets manager for sensitive values.
concepts.example: Start the local Compose stack, configure a non-secret connection and document how a production secrets backend would supply credentials.

concepts.name: Monitoring, debugging and testing
concepts.explanation: Use Grid, Graph, Gantt and task logs to investigate stuck DAGs, scheduler problems, pool exhaustion and zombie tasks. airflow tasks test and airflow dags test support local debugging. Test custom Operators/Hooks and validate imports, cycles, reachability and CI behavior before deployment.
concepts.example: Add DAG integrity tests and one unit test for a custom component; make CI fail on an import error and record a local task-test command.

Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Phase 3 · Streaming and CDC with Kafka
lessons.why: Ingest changes as durable ordered events, understand delivery guarantees and schemas, and operate a CDC path from a transactional database into a lake or warehouse.
lessons.summary: Ingest changes as durable ordered events, understand delivery guarantees and schemas, and operate a CDC path from a transactional database into a lake or warehouse.

concepts.name: Kafka foundations
concepts.explanation: Topics contain partitions; offsets identify records and ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across a topic. Brokers form clusters and replicate partitions with a replication factor and in-sync replicas. Producers choose partitioning and acknowledgements (acks=0/1/all); consumer groups distribute partitions and rebalance. Retention can delete by time/size or compact by key.
concepts.example: Produce keyed customer events and show that matching keys retain partition order while unrelated partitions have no global ordering.

concepts.name: Delivery semantics
concepts.explanation: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once depend on when offsets are committed and what is transactional. Idempotent producers reduce duplicate writes; consumers choose automatic or manual commits. Kafka transactions coordinate records and offsets but do not make arbitrary external side effects exactly once.
concepts.example: Crash a consumer before and after committing an offset, observe possible replay, and make a downstream write idempotent.

concepts.name: Schema management
concepts.explanation: A schema registry governs independently deployed producer and consumer contracts. Backward, forward and full compatibility define which old/new readers and writers interoperate. Avro, Protobuf and JSON Schema trade compactness, tooling and flexibility; schema evolution must be planned before breaking downstream readers.
concepts.example: Add an optional field under a chosen compatibility rule and test old and new consumer fixtures.

concepts.name: Change data capture
concepts.explanation: CDC reads a database transaction log instead of repeatedly polling tables. Debezium connectors emit before/after images, operation type and source metadata. Initial snapshots and incremental capture have different behavior; handle deletes, source schema changes and out-of-order events explicitly.
concepts.example: Capture inserts, updates and deletes from a disposable PostgreSQL table and verify event key, operation and source position.

concepts.name: Kafka Connect
concepts.explanation: Source connectors publish records and sink connectors write topics to a lake or warehouse. Debezium is a source connector. Converters select serialization; Single Message Transforms make lightweight record changes. Connector plugins and configurations need versioning and safe secrets.
concepts.example: Configure a local connector pair with a converter and one SMT, validate connector status and preserve a raw event for audit.

concepts.name: Stream processing
concepts.explanation: Choose Spark Structured Streaming or Flink for a practical project and know the other exists. Distinguish stateless from stateful operations, tumbling/sliding/session windows, event-time watermarks and late data, stream-stream/stream-static joins, and checkpointing for fault tolerance.
concepts.example: Compute a windowed event count with a watermark, join a stream to static reference data and restart from a checkpoint.

concepts.name: Architecture patterns
concepts.explanation: A CDC-to-Kafka-to-lakehouse path commonly lands raw events in a bronze layer. Kappa emphasizes a stream as the processing source; Lambda combines batch and streaming paths. Fan-out lets independent consumers use the same CDC stream without coupling their processing.
concepts.example: Design a CDC event path with two independent consumers and state which records are retained for replay.

concepts.name: Operations and debugging
concepts.explanation: Monitor consumer lag and use kafka-topics, kafka-console-consumer/producer and kafka-consumer-groups to inspect the system. Diagnose rebalance storms, poison-pill messages and connector crashes; apply backpressure when downstream processing is slower than producers.
concepts.example: Create a small local topic, inspect group lag, introduce a malformed record and document a quarantine/recovery strategy.

lessons.title: Phase 4 · Lakehouse formats and storage internals
lessons.why: Understand what happens beneath analytical tables, and how transactional table formats, catalogs and query engines make object storage usable for evolving batch and streaming workloads.
lessons.summary: Understand what happens beneath analytical tables, and how transactional table formats, catalogs and query engines make object storage usable for evolving batch and streaming workloads.

concepts.name: File formats
concepts.explanation: Row-oriented formats suit record-at-a-time access; columnar formats suit analytical scans. Parquet stores row groups, column chunks, pages and footer metadata; column statistics enable pruning and predicate pushdown. Snappy, Gzip and Zstd trade compression ratio for CPU; dictionary and run-length encoding exploit repeated values. ORC is another analytical format and Avro is common for CDC events.
concepts.example: Inspect a Parquet file's schema and row groups, then compare a narrow projection with a full-row scan.

concepts.name: Why table formats matter
concepts.explanation: Raw Parquet on a filesystem becomes difficult as tables grow: small files increase metadata and planning overhead, while concurrent writers can conflict without transaction coordination.
concepts.example: Write many tiny files, measure listing/planning overhead, then compact them.

concepts.name: Iceberg and Delta internals
concepts.explanation: Iceberg and Delta add metadata and transaction layers over object storage. Iceberg manifests, manifest lists and snapshots describe files; both formats use optimistic concurrency for ACID-like updates. Time travel queries a prior snapshot; schema evolution avoids rewriting all data. Iceberg supports partition evolution and hidden partitioning.
concepts.example: Create snapshots, evolve a schema and query the prior snapshot; explain which metadata enables the operation.

concepts.name: Table maintenance
concepts.explanation: Compaction merges small files; snapshot expiration or vacuuming removes eligible historical data. Sorting or Z-ordering improves data skipping for selected query patterns; Iceberg sort orders and manifest rewrites keep metadata useful. Retention must be balanced with recovery and compliance needs.
concepts.example: Generate small files, compact them, compare file counts and query scan metrics, then describe safe history retention.

concepts.name: Catalogs
concepts.explanation: A catalog resolves table names to metadata locations. Hive Metastore is a traditional option; AWS Glue is managed; Nessie provides Git-like versioning for Iceberg; REST catalogs expose a service interface used by a growing ecosystem.
concepts.example: Register a table through a catalog and show that consumers resolve its metadata without hard-coded file paths.

concepts.name: Query engines
concepts.explanation: Trino/Presto use coordinator and worker roles plus connectors to query sources. Federated SQL can combine Postgres, Parquet on S3 and a warehouse. Engines use table metadata to skip files and partitions; Spark suits heavy ETL while Trino suits interactive/federated SQL workloads.
concepts.example: Run one small analytical query in Spark and Trino or compare plans on paper, explaining workload, latency and resource trade-offs.

concepts.name: Lakehouse architecture
concepts.explanation: Map bronze raw, silver conformed and gold aggregated data to Iceberg or Delta tables. Choose partitioning based on query predicates while avoiding over-partitioning. Batch and streaming writers may land in the same table only with a compatible commit and layout strategy.
concepts.example: Design a medallion table layout for time-stamped events and justify partitions, file sizing and batch/stream coordination.

concepts.name: Operations and platform fluency
concepts.explanation: Inspect snapshots and files metadata tables to diagnose small-file and catalog issues. Metadata size and catalog choice affect cost and performance over time. As an optional weekend extension, use Databricks Community Edition if currently available at no cost to ingest data, create Delta tables and schedule a Databricks Job; the core learning path must not depend on that service.
concepts.example: Write a table health report from metadata and outline a compact/expire plan; if a free Databricks environment is available, reproduce one medallion pipeline there.

Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Phase 5 · Transformation and modeling with dbt + Kimball
lessons.why: Turn raw tables into tested, documented models that answer business questions, with incremental processing and dimensional-modeling choices that remain correct as data changes.
lessons.summary: Turn raw tables into tested, documented models that answer business questions, with incremental processing and dimensional-modeling choices that remain correct as data changes.

concepts.name: dbt project and DAG
concepts.explanation: A dbt project organizes models, sources, seeds, snapshots, macros, tests, exposures and analyses. view, table, incremental and ephemeral materializations trade freshness, compute and reuse. ref() and source() create dependency edges; dbt build runs the selected resource graph with tests, while dbt run and dbt test focus on transformations and checks.
concepts.example: Create source, staging and mart models linked with source() and ref(), then inspect the generated DAG.

concepts.name: Incremental models
concepts.explanation: Append, merge, delete+insert and insert_overwrite strategies suit different warehouses and data shapes. is_incremental() must support both incremental and full-refresh execution. Choose a unique key and handle late-arriving or updated records; a flawed filter can silently omit corrections.
concepts.example: Run an incremental model twice with a late update and duplicate key, then prove both runs match the expected full-refresh result.

concepts.name: Snapshots and slowly changing dimensions
concepts.explanation: Snapshots preserve mutable source records over time. Timestamp strategy uses an updated-at field; check strategy compares selected columns. Implement SCD Type 2 with validity intervals and current-row indicators, and explain when Types 1, 2 or 3 are appropriate.
concepts.example: Track a customer's changing address and show current and historical rows with correct validity boundaries.

concepts.name: Testing, docs and exposures
concepts.explanation: Built-in generic tests include unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships; singular and generic custom tests encode domain rules. dbt docs generate builds documentation and DAG visualization; exposures describe downstream dashboards and applications.
concepts.example: Add generic and singular tests, generate docs and declare one downstream exposure.

concepts.name: Dimensional modeling
concepts.explanation: Facts and dimensions begin with a declared grain. Measures can be additive, semi-additive or non-additive. Star and snowflake schemas organize analysis differently; conformed dimensions align multiple fact tables/marts. Surrogate and natural keys, plus bridge tables, address identity and many-to-many relationships.
concepts.example: Model orders and order lines at distinct grains, add a conformed customer dimension and a bridge for a many-to-many tag relationship.

concepts.name: Consumer-focused contracts
concepts.explanation: Data contracts define expected schema and semantics between producers and consumers. Gold models should answer business questions rather than mirror source convenience. Consistent naming and versioned contracts make breaking changes explicit and reviewable.
concepts.example: Write a gold-layer contract for a named business question and test a deliberate breaking schema change.

concepts.name: Macros and reuse
concepts.explanation: Jinja macros centralize repeated SQL patterns; packages.yml declares dependencies such as dbt-utils. vars pass environment or run-specific values. Abstraction should reduce duplication without obscuring generated SQL.
concepts.example: Create a small tested macro, pin a package version and inspect compiled SQL for two variable configurations.

concepts.name: Orchestration and CI
concepts.explanation: Airflow can run dbt through a BashOperator, Cosmos or dbt Cloud API. dbt build --select and state:modified+ support selective work; Slim CI checks changed models and downstream dependents before deployment.
concepts.example: Create a pull-request validation that builds changed models and their dependents against a disposable target, then documents promotion criteria.

lessons.title: Phase 6 · Data quality and observability
lessons.why: Make data trust measurable: detect failures close to their source, trace downstream impact and route actionable alerts instead of discovering silent corruption through consumers.
lessons.summary: Make data trust measurable: detect failures close to their source, trace downstream impact and route actionable alerts instead of discovering silent corruption through consumers.

concepts.name: Quality as a discipline
concepts.explanation: Bad data can fail loudly or silently. Schema changes, upstream defects, late or missing data and duplicates are common causes. Shift checks earlier so invalid records are caught before they reach consumers.
concepts.example: Inject a duplicate and a missing required field at ingestion and compare early rejection with a downstream report.

concepts.name: Quality dimensions
concepts.explanation: Completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, freshness/timeliness and accuracy describe different failure modes; choose checks that match the data contract and use case.
concepts.example: Define one measurable check and an example failure for each dimension on a small orders table.

concepts.name: Great Expectations and alternatives
concepts.explanation: Expectations and Expectation Suites describe assertions; Validation Results record outcomes. Common checks cover nulls, ranges, uniqueness and row-count bounds. Data Docs report results; Checkpoints combine expectations, data and actions. Soda, dbt tests and Deequ are alternatives with different integration models.
concepts.example: Create a local suite, validate good and bad fixtures, review the result and compare an equivalent dbt test.

concepts.name: Data contracts
concepts.explanation: Contracts formalize producer-consumer expectations and can be enforced at ingestion or layer boundaries. Version contracts and define a compatibility process for breaking changes.
concepts.example: Publish a versioned event contract and reject a breaking producer change in a test.

concepts.name: Lineage
concepts.explanation: Lineage explains upstream causes and downstream blast radius. Table-level and column-level lineage have different resolution. OpenLineage standardizes lineage events; Marquez is a reference backend. Airflow and dbt can emit or expose lineage for connected workflows.
concepts.example: Trace a gold metric to its source columns and identify the downstream dashboard affected by one upstream change.

concepts.name: Monitoring and alerting
concepts.explanation: Freshness catches stale tables; volume catches row-count drops/spikes; schema drift catches changed columns or types; distribution monitoring can surface anomalies. Route alerts with owner, impact and runbook context to avoid alert fatigue.
concepts.example: Create freshness, volume and schema checks on generated daily partitions and route only actionable failures to a mock alert.

concepts.name: Lightweight anomaly detection
concepts.explanation: Rolling averages and standard-deviation thresholds can detect simple changes. Rule-based, statistical and ML-based methods differ in complexity and explainability; use simple rules when sufficient.
concepts.example: Compare a fixed threshold and rolling baseline on a synthetic seasonal series with one injected anomaly.

concepts.name: Operational quality checks
concepts.explanation: Place checks after ingestion, after transformation or both depending on the failure and recovery boundary. Fail fast for invalid data that must not propagate; quarantine recoverable bad records. Connect Airflow check failures to real alert callbacks and track quality measures over time.
concepts.example: Build an Airflow-style validation path that quarantines malformed records, fails a critical contract violation, emits an alert and stores trend metrics.

lessons.title: Phase 7 · Cloud and infrastructure
lessons.why: Package, deploy and operate data workloads with reproducible infrastructure, least privilege, safe delivery and cost awareness; choose one cloud rather than surveying every provider.
lessons.summary: Package, deploy and operate data workloads with reproducible infrastructure, least privilege, safe delivery and cost awareness; choose one cloud rather than surveying every provider.

concepts.name: Docker in depth
concepts.explanation: Multi-stage builds reduce production image size; layer caching speeds repeated builds. Volumes persist container data, while bind mounts connect host paths. Bridge networking enables container communication; Compose healthchecks, depends_on conditions and resource limits shape local stacks.
concepts.example: Build a multi-stage worker image, demonstrate a healthcheck and distinguish a named volume from a bind mount.

concepts.name: Kubernetes basics
concepts.explanation: Pods run containers; Deployments manage replicas; Services provide stable access; ConfigMaps and Secrets supply configuration. Jobs and CronJobs run finite or scheduled work; Namespaces isolate projects. Resource requests and limits affect placement and throttling. Practice kubectl get, describe, logs and exec with minikube or kind.
concepts.example: Deploy a small CronJob locally, inspect its logs and explain a deliberately too-low CPU limit.

concepts.name: Kubernetes for data workloads
concepts.explanation: Airflow's KubernetesExecutor runs tasks as pods; Spark-on-Kubernetes runs driver and executor pods. Persistent Volumes and Claims provide storage for stateful workloads. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is a conceptual starting point for scaling replicas based on metrics.
concepts.example: Sketch the Airflow task-pod and Spark driver/executor resources, including storage and resource requests.

concepts.name: Terraform foundations
concepts.explanation: Providers connect Terraform to APIs; resources create managed objects and data sources read existing ones. State (.tfstate) tracks objects and should use remote storage and locking when shared. plan previews changes before apply; variables, outputs and modules support reuse. Detect drift by comparing configuration and real infrastructure.
concepts.example: Create a small local or sandbox plan, review its proposed changes before apply and explain remote state locking and drift.

concepts.name: One cloud end to end
concepts.explanation: Choose AWS or GCP. Learn S3/GCS buckets, lifecycle policies and storage classes; EC2/Cloud Run plus Lambda/Cloud Functions as a serverless option; IAM roles versus users and policies with least privilege and service accounts; VPCs, subnets, security groups/firewall rules; and managed RDS/Cloud SQL, MSK/Confluent Cloud, EMR/Dataproc services.
concepts.example: Draw a least-privilege architecture for a batch pipeline on one provider and identify each storage, compute, identity, network and managed-data boundary.

concepts.name: CI/CD for data pipelines
concepts.explanation: CI runs linting, unit tests, DAG validation and dbt tests on every pull request. CD builds, tests and deploys. GitHub Actions or GitLab CI organize workflows, jobs, steps and runners. Test DAGs in CI and use dbt build --select state:modified+ where supported. Stage and validate data before promotion.
concepts.example: Create a CI workflow for SQL/Python checks, DAG validation and changed dbt models; require staging validation before production promotion.

concepts.name: Secrets and configuration
concepts.explanation: Never hardcode credentials. Use environment variables for local configuration and cloud secrets managers or Vault for production secrets; inject secrets safely into containers/pods. Separate environment configuration without copying business logic.
concepts.example: Rotate a test credential, confirm logs and image layers do not contain it, and load distinct development and staging configuration.

concepts.name: Cost and operations
concepts.explanation: Read a cloud bill and identify storage, compute, network and idle-resource drivers. Right-size executors and pods; spot/preemptible instances can reduce costs for retryable non-critical batch workloads, but not every task is safe to interrupt.
concepts.example: Estimate costs for a small batch workload, show one right-sizing change and document which tasks could safely use interruptible compute.

lessons.title: Phase 8 · ML engineering and MLOps
lessons.why: Connect reliable data engineering to reproducible model training and serving, while making feature correctness, model lifecycle and production feedback explicit.
lessons.summary: Connect reliable data engineering to reproducible model training and serving, while making feature correctness, model lifecycle and production feedback explicit.

concepts.name: Feature engineering pipelines
concepts.explanation: Feature pipelines are data pipelines with an ML consumer. Batch and online/real-time feature computation differ in latency and freshness. Feature stores support reuse but must address training-serving skew and point-in-time correctness. Feast models entities and feature views over offline and online stores; point-in-time joins prevent future information leaking into training.
concepts.example: Build a point-in-time feature join and show how a future event would create leakage.

concepts.name: Model training pipelines
concepts.explanation: Structure training as extraction, features, train, evaluate and register steps. Reproducibility pins data, code and hyperparameters together. Grid/random search provide baselines; Bayesian optimization may be worth the extra complexity for expensive searches. Cross-validation should be represented in the pipeline, not hidden in an ad hoc notebook.
concepts.example: Build a versioned training DAG with a fixed data snapshot and compare a small grid search with one baseline.

concepts.name: Experiment tracking and registry
concepts.explanation: MLflow Tracking stores parameters, metrics and artifacts; its Model Registry supports lifecycle states such as staging, production and archived. Record metrics, hyperparameters, data version/hash and environment so a run can be compared and reproduced.
concepts.example: Log two training runs with data hashes and promote only the evaluated artifact through explicit registry stages.

concepts.name: Deployment patterns
concepts.explanation: Batch inference processes a scheduled dataset; online inference serves requests with tighter latency needs. Serve through FastAPI and a container when appropriate. Shadow and canary deployments compare or gradually expose a model before full rollout.
concepts.example: Deploy a local model endpoint and compare batch output with a shadow request path before routing traffic.

concepts.name: Monitoring and drift
concepts.explanation: Data drift changes input distributions; concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and outcomes. Monitor prediction distributions as well as uptime and latency. Retraining may be scheduled or triggered by drift, but requires a verified policy. Capture ground truth to evaluate real-world performance and avoid unsafe feedback loops.
concepts.example: Simulate a distribution shift, report prediction changes, then compare a scheduled retrain trigger with a ground-truth-confirmed trigger.

concepts.name: Integration back into DE
concepts.explanation: Airflow can orchestrate retrain, evaluate, register and deploy. Predictions can return to a gold-layer table in the medallion architecture. Version data, features, model and code as one reproducible unit.
concepts.example: Orchestrate a local train/evaluate/register flow and write versioned predictions to a gold table with lineage back to its feature and model versions.

lessons.title: Phase 9 · LLM and GenAI engineering
lessons.why: Understand enough model architecture and evaluation to build grounded language-model systems that fit into a data platform, without treating a model response as proof of correctness.
lessons.summary: Understand enough model architecture and evaluation to build grounded language-model systems that fit into a data platform, without treating a model response as proof of correctness.

concepts.name: Deep learning foundations
concepts.explanation: Perceptrons, activation functions, backpropagation and gradient descent provide conceptual fluency without derivation-heavy mathematics. CNNs and RNNs address image and sequence tasks; transformers largely replaced RNNs for many sequence workloads. Batch size, learning rate, Adam/SGD, dropout and weight decay shape training.
concepts.example: Explain a forward pass and gradient update in a tiny network, then identify when a CNN, RNN or transformer is a reasonable architecture.

concepts.name: Transformer architecture
concepts.explanation: Self-attention is the core interaction mechanism. Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder designs correspond broadly to BERT-, GPT- and T5-style tasks. Positional encoding and multi-head attention help represent order and multiple relation patterns; this vocabulary helps interpret model cards.
concepts.example: Trace input tokens through positional information and multi-head self-attention, and identify the model family in a model card.

concepts.name: LLM-specific skills
concepts.explanation: Pretraining, fine-tuning and instruction tuning change different parts of model behavior. LoRA/QLoRA adapt fewer parameters than full fine-tuning; prompting may be preferable when data, cost or maintenance do not justify training. Few-shot and structured-output prompts are practical tools. In-context learning uses examples in the prompt without changing model weights.
concepts.example: Compare a prompt-only baseline with a small structured-output and few-shot evaluation; explain when adaptation would be justified.

concepts.name: Evaluation and responsible AI
concepts.explanation: Benchmark suites, LLM-as-judge and human evaluation measure different properties; plausible prose is not evaluation. Hallucination can be mitigated with grounded retrieval and calibrated uncertainty signals, but not eliminated by a single prompt. Discuss bias and safety at a practical level and set clear product limits.
concepts.example: Create a small golden set, score grounded answers and unsupported questions, and review failures with a human rubric.

concepts.name: LLM and RAG stack
concepts.explanation: Embeddings map text to vectors; cosine similarity and dot product rank candidates. pgvector, Qdrant and Weaviate are vector-storage options. Fixed-size, semantic and overlapping chunks have different context trade-offs. Dense, hybrid dense+BM25 and reranked retrieval are alternatives. A RAG pipeline ingests, chunks, embeds, stores, retrieves and generates; evaluate recall@k separately from answer quality.
concepts.example: Build a local RAG baseline and compare retrieval recall@k with grounded answer quality on the same held-out questions.

concepts.name: Agents, lighter touch
concepts.explanation: Tools use function calling to invoke bounded actions. A single agent with tools differs from multi-agent handoff in complexity and coordination. Identify practical DE/AI uses before adopting agents; LangChain/LangGraph are options, as is a lean custom workflow.
concepts.example: Add one read-only data-quality tool to a bounded assistant, require approval for changes and explain why a simple workflow may be safer than a multi-agent system.

lessons.title: Phase 10 · System design and interview preparation
lessons.why: Use the earlier phases and your own projects to communicate architecture trade-offs, solve practical data-engineering exercises and prepare for DE or AI engineering interviews.
lessons.summary: Use the earlier phases and your own projects to communicate architecture trade-offs, solve practical data-engineering exercises and prepare for DE or AI engineering interviews.

concepts.name: System design framework
concepts.explanation: Clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, deep-dive into the critical path and explain trade-offs. Batch and streaming choices depend on throughput, latency and correctness; push back on requirements when the constraints conflict. Practice back-of-envelope data-volume estimates aloud.
concepts.example: Estimate daily event volume and storage for a CDC service, state assumptions, and revise the design when latency requirements change.

concepts.name: Case studies
concepts.explanation: Practice a CDC path from Postgres through Kafka into a lake; a real-time analytics dashboard; a domain data warehouse; a feature store/ML pipeline; a data-quality and observability service; and multi-source ingestion into a medallion architecture.
concepts.example: Draw one end-to-end design and include failure recovery, idempotency, ownership and measurable acceptance criteria.

concepts.name: Trade-off articulation
concepts.explanation: CAP theorem is a practical vocabulary for consistency and availability under partitions, not a universal product label. Discuss cost, performance and complexity; managed service versus custom build; and resolve “it depends” by naming the workload and decision criteria.
concepts.example: Compare managed Kafka with a self-managed cluster for a stated team size, throughput, availability target and budget.

concepts.name: SQL interview fluency
concepts.explanation: Use window functions, CTEs and complex joins under time pressure. Explain query optimization by identifying scans, cardinality and indexes or layout; practice through StrataScratch, DataLemur or LeetCode database exercises.
concepts.example: Solve a window-function query from a small fixture and explain why an intentionally slow version scans too much data.

concepts.name: Python interview fluency
concepts.explanation: Manipulate records without relying on pandas, refresh OOP in interview language and write readable code on a shared document or whiteboard without autocomplete.
concepts.example: Implement a streaming aggregation with standard Python, tests and clear handling for empty and malformed input.

concepts.name: Pipeline design coding
concepts.explanation: Practice implementing a simple ETL script, answering idempotency and error-handling questions, and completing documented take-home-style exercises end to end.
concepts.example: Build a small restartable ETL function with validation, retry-safe writes, tests and a concise README.

concepts.name: Behavioral preparation
concepts.explanation: Prepare STAR stories for three or four strong projects: production failure, a design decision you would change and learning quickly. Explain why decisions were made, not only what you built, and prepare thoughtful questions for interviewers.
concepts.example: Write three project stories with situation, task, action, result and one reflection; support each with evidence from the project.

concepts.name: Mock interviews
concepts.explanation: Practice with a peer, mentor or recorded self-explanation across SQL, live coding, system design and behavioral formats. Run a specific retrospective after each mock for fumbles, over-explaining and missed clarification questions.
concepts.example: Record a short mock design, score it with a rubric and turn the two largest gaps into follow-up exercises.

concepts.name: Company and role-specific preparation
concepts.explanation: Research target-company technology stacks from job postings and engineering blogs; map current skills to role expectations and flag gaps early. Tailor project explanations to DE depth or AI/RAG depth without overstating experience.
concepts.example: Choose a real role description, map evidence-backed skills to requirements, and prepare two versions of a project walkthrough.

lessons.why: Match the learning objective to the user problem and target data.
lessons.summary: Match the learning objective to the user problem and target data.

concepts.explanation: Learn a mapping from features to known targets; labels define the task and can contain errors.
concepts.example: Predict a category from labeled support messages.

concepts.name: Regression versus classification
concepts.explanation: Regression predicts a numeric quantity; classification predicts discrete categories.
concepts.example: Predict delivery duration versus whether a delivery is late.

concepts.name: Baselines and losses
concepts.explanation: A baseline establishes minimum useful performance; a training loss provides an optimizable objective.
concepts.example: Compare a majority-class baseline with logistic regression.

lessons.title: Train/validation/test, cross-validation and leakage
lessons.why: Measure generalization using data the model and preprocessing have not seen.
lessons.summary: Measure generalization using data the model and preprocessing have not seen.

concepts.name: Splits
concepts.explanation: Training fits parameters, validation chooses designs and testing estimates final performance.
concepts.example: Reserve a test set before choosing the regularization strength.

concepts.name: Cross-validation
concepts.explanation: Repeated train/validation folds estimate variability; groups and time ordering may require special splitters.
concepts.example: Keep records from one customer in the same fold.

concepts.name: Leakage
concepts.explanation: Information from evaluation data or future events can inflate scores.
concepts.example: Fit a scaler inside a Pipeline on training folds only.

lessons.summary: Convert messy records into features consistently during training and inference.

concepts.example: Standardize numeric features and one-hot encode categories with unknown-category handling.

concepts.name: Feature engineering
concepts.explanation: Transformations capture useful information but should respect availability at prediction time.
concepts.example: Extract weekday from a timestamp known before a prediction.

concepts.name: Pipelines
concepts.explanation: ColumnTransformer and Pipeline bundle transformations with the estimator to prevent drift and leakage.
concepts.example: Save one fitted pipeline instead of separate manually applied transformations.

lessons.title: Linear/logistic regression and gradient descent
lessons.why: Understand simple models before relying on complex ones.
lessons.summary: Understand simple models before relying on complex ones.

concepts.name: Linear regression
concepts.explanation: A weighted feature sum predicts a continuous value; squared error penalizes large residuals.
concepts.example: Fit y≈3x+2 with noisy generated points.

concepts.name: Logistic regression
concepts.explanation: A sigmoid or softmax converts linear scores into class probabilities; cross-entropy trains the classifier.
concepts.example: Predict a binary label from two numeric features.

concepts.name: Gradient descent
concepts.explanation: Learning rate controls update size; an excessive rate can diverge.
concepts.example: Plot loss for small and excessive step sizes on the same dataset.

lessons.title: Trees, random forests and boosting
lessons.why: Compare nonlinear baselines and recognize how ensembles reduce different errors.
lessons.summary: Compare nonlinear baselines and recognize how ensembles reduce different errors.

concepts.name: Decision trees
concepts.explanation: Trees partition feature space using split rules and can overfit deeply.
concepts.example: Limit max_depth and compare training with validation accuracy.

concepts.name: Random forests
concepts.explanation: Bootstrap sampling and randomized features diversify trees before averaging.
concepts.example: Compare a single tree and a forest across random seeds.

concepts.name: Boosting
concepts.explanation: Sequential weak learners focus on remaining error; learning rate and tree size control complexity.
concepts.example: Evaluate HistGradientBoosting on a small tabular dataset.

lessons.title: kNN, SVM, clustering and PCA
lessons.why: Choose methods based on geometry, labels and dimensionality.
lessons.summary: Choose methods based on geometry, labels and dimensionality.

concepts.name: kNN and SVM
concepts.explanation: Neighbors depend on distance and scaling; SVM seeks a separating margin and may use kernels.
concepts.example: Compare scaled and unscaled kNN on the same features.

concepts.name: Clustering
concepts.explanation: Unsupervised grouping finds structure without targets; cluster IDs are not ground-truth labels.
concepts.example: Run k-means on synthetic blobs and inspect sensitivity to k.

concepts.name: PCA
concepts.explanation: Principal components compress directions of variance; high variance is not necessarily predictive information.
concepts.example: Project standardized digits features to two components for visualization.

lessons.title: Bias/variance, regularization and tuning
lessons.why: Improve validation behavior rather than merely maximizing training scores.
lessons.summary: Improve validation behavior rather than merely maximizing training scores.

concepts.name: Bias and variance
concepts.explanation: Underfitting misses useful structure; overfitting captures noise and unstable patterns.
concepts.example: Compare learning curves for shallow and deep trees.

concepts.name: Regularization
concepts.explanation: Penalties or structural constraints restrict complexity; stronger regularization is not always better.
concepts.example: Sweep logistic regression C across a small logarithmic grid.

concepts.name: Hyperparameter tuning
concepts.explanation: Search uses validation folds, never repeatedly exposed test data.
concepts.example: Compare three candidate settings with cross-validation then evaluate once.

lessons.title: Imbalance, metrics, calibration and error analysis
lessons.why: Measure the mistakes that matter and distinguish probability quality from label accuracy.
lessons.summary: Measure the mistakes that matter and distinguish probability quality from label accuracy.

concepts.name: Classification metrics
concepts.explanation: Precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC answer different questions; accuracy hides rare-class failures.
concepts.example: A classifier predicting only the majority class can still have high accuracy.

concepts.name: Calibration and thresholds
concepts.explanation: Calibration compares probabilities with frequencies; thresholds trade false positives against false negatives.
concepts.example: Choose a threshold on validation data and evaluate its confusion matrix.

concepts.name: Error analysis
concepts.explanation: Inspect error slices and mislabeled samples; metrics alone do not reveal causes.
concepts.example: Group errors by feature range and compare class-weighted training.

lessons.title: Model persistence, inference and data drift
lessons.why: Serve the same preprocessing and model version that you evaluated.
lessons.summary: Serve the same preprocessing and model version that you evaluated.

concepts.name: Persistence
concepts.explanation: Persist the complete fitted pipeline and version metadata; pickle-like formats are unsafe from untrusted sources.
concepts.example: Load only an artifact your own training job produced.

concepts.name: Inference contracts
concepts.explanation: Validate feature schema and define batch and single-example outputs.
concepts.example: Reject a missing required feature instead of silently shifting column order.

concepts.name: Drift
concepts.explanation: Feature or target distributions can change after deployment; alerts need reference windows and action plans.
concepts.example: Compare current feature histograms with training statistics.

lessons.title: Column transformers, nested validation and tuning budgets
lessons.why: Tune models while keeping preprocessing and model selection inside a leakage-safe validation procedure.
lessons.summary: Tune models while keeping preprocessing and model selection inside a leakage-safe validation procedure.

concepts.name: Per-column preprocessing
concepts.explanation: Different feature types need explicit transformations that are fit only on the training fold.
concepts.example: Impute and scale numeric columns while one-hot encoding categorical columns in one ColumnTransformer.

concepts.name: Pipeline fit boundaries
concepts.explanation: A Pipeline ensures fit-dependent preprocessing is repeated within each validation split instead of learning from all rows.
concepts.example: Compare a deliberately leaked feature selector with the same selector placed inside the cross-validation pipeline.

concepts.name: Search-space design
concepts.explanation: A bounded search expresses hypotheses about influential parameters rather than trying every possible combination.
concepts.example: Compare a small logarithmic range of regularisation strengths instead of a huge dense grid.

concepts.name: Nested validation
concepts.explanation: An outer validation estimates the complete model-selection procedure while inner validation chooses hyperparameters.
concepts.example: Use two outer folds and two inner folds on a tiny synthetic dataset and record which observations each stage sees.

concepts.name: Search accounting
concepts.explanation: Compare procedures under similar computational budgets and retain validation results, seeds and configuration.
concepts.example: Log each candidate score and runtime; keep a final untouched test set for the selected procedure.

lessons.title: Class imbalance, decision thresholds and calibration
lessons.why: Translate classifier scores into a defensible decision rule rather than relying on accuracy or a default threshold.
lessons.summary: Translate classifier scores into a defensible decision rule rather than relying on accuracy or a default threshold.

concepts.name: Base rate and accuracy
concepts.explanation: A rare positive class makes a majority predictor look accurate without solving the intended detection problem.
concepts.example: For 1% positives, calculate the accuracy and recall of predicting every example negative.

concepts.name: Precision-recall tradeoff
concepts.explanation: Changing a threshold changes the set of predicted positives and therefore false-positive and false-negative counts.
concepts.example: Compute a confusion matrix at thresholds 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 on a fixed score vector.

concepts.name: Class weights and resampling
concepts.explanation: Weighting or resampling changes the training objective or distribution and must be confined to training folds.
concepts.example: Compare weighted and unweighted logistic regression without modifying the validation class balance.

concepts.name: Calibration meaning
concepts.explanation: A calibrated probability should match observed outcome frequency for similar scores under the evaluation distribution.
concepts.example: Group predictions near 0.8 and compare their average score with the observed positive fraction.

concepts.name: Decision cost and threshold validation
concepts.explanation: Choose thresholds on validation data using a declared utility or capacity limit; the test set must not tune the decision.
concepts.example: Select a threshold meeting a review budget and evaluate that fixed threshold once on the test split.

lessons.title: Permutation importance, partial dependence and error slices
lessons.why: Explain a model carefully and identify which examples fail without confusing predictive association with causation.
lessons.summary: Explain a model carefully and identify which examples fail without confusing predictive association with causation.

concepts.name: Held-out permutation importance
concepts.explanation: Shuffling one feature estimates how much a fitted model relies on it for a chosen metric and evaluation dataset.
concepts.example: Shuffle a useful numeric column in held-out data and compare the score drop with a random-noise column.

concepts.name: Correlated features
concepts.explanation: Importance can be shared or hidden among interchangeable features, so a low individual score does not prove irrelevance.
concepts.example: Duplicate a predictive column and compare individual permutation scores before and after duplication.

concepts.name: Partial dependence assumptions
concepts.explanation: A partial-dependence plot averages predictions while varying selected features and can query unrealistic combinations.
concepts.example: Plot a model response while checking whether the varied values are plausible for the observed subgroup.

concepts.name: Error slices
concepts.explanation: Aggregate quality can hide failures in specific sources, lengths or groups; require sample counts and uncertainty.
concepts.example: Compare false-negative rates for short versus long synthetic records and display each slice size.

concepts.name: Association versus intervention
concepts.explanation: A predictive explanation describes model behaviour, not the result of changing the real world.
concepts.example: Explain why a feature importance for support history does not establish what happens if support history is artificially changed.

lessons.title: SVM margins, kernels, C and feature scale
lessons.why: Understand what changes when a linear classifier becomes a kernel method and why preprocessing matters.
lessons.summary: Understand what changes when a linear classifier becomes a kernel method and why preprocessing matters.

concepts.name: Separating margin
concepts.explanation: A maximum-margin classifier chooses a boundary using support vectors close to the margin rather than every point equally.
concepts.example: Plot a two-dimensional linear decision boundary and highlight the fitted support vectors.

concepts.name: Soft-margin C
concepts.explanation: C controls the cost of violations relative to the regularisation objective and should be tuned within validation.
concepts.example: Compare a small and a large C on a generated dataset with one mislabeled outlier.

concepts.name: Kernel similarity
concepts.explanation: A kernel defines an implicit feature-space similarity; an RBF kernel depends on distance and its bandwidth parameter.
concepts.example: Compute exp(-gamma*distance_squared) for two distances and two gamma values.

concepts.name: Scale and preprocessing
concepts.explanation: Feature units affect distances and therefore kernel similarity; scale within a training pipeline to avoid leakage.
concepts.example: Rescale one feature by 100 and compare unscaled with pipeline-scaled performance.

concepts.name: Compute and probability caveats
concepts.explanation: Kernel methods may become expensive as training size grows, and a decision score is not automatically a calibrated probability.
concepts.example: Record fit time for two small sample sizes and report decision scores separately from any calibrated estimate.

lessons.title: Time-series validation and anomaly-detection baselines
lessons.why: Handle ordered observations and rare events without training on future information.
lessons.summary: Handle ordered observations and rare events without training on future information.

concepts.name: Forecast horizon and lag features
concepts.explanation: A forecasting target specifies how far into the future to predict; lagged features must exist at the decision time.
concepts.example: Predict tomorrow's count using yesterday's count rather than a rolling mean that includes tomorrow.

concepts.name: Walk-forward evaluation
concepts.explanation: Training expands or rolls through time and validation follows it, respecting the intended deployment chronology.
concepts.example: Evaluate three chronological windows and compare with a shuffled split that looks unrealistically strong.

concepts.name: Seasonal naive baseline
concepts.explanation: Simple repetition or moving averages provide a meaningful baseline before adding a learned forecaster.
concepts.example: Predict a day using the same weekday one week earlier and calculate mean absolute error.

concepts.name: Anomaly score versus label
concepts.explanation: An unsupervised detector produces an unusualness score; the alert threshold depends on operating needs and validation evidence.
concepts.example: Rank points by IsolationForest score and choose a review threshold on a separate validation period.

concepts.name: Alert evaluation
concepts.explanation: Evaluate event coverage, false alerts and review volume rather than assuming every rare point is useful to a user.
concepts.example: Group adjacent anomalous windows into events and compare event recall with raw pointwise recall.

lessons.title: K-means, density clustering and PCA diagnostics
lessons.why: Interpret unsupervised outputs in terms of assumptions instead of treating every cluster label as a discovered truth.
lessons.summary: Interpret unsupervised outputs in terms of assumptions instead of treating every cluster label as a discovered truth.

concepts.name: K-means objective
concepts.explanation: K-means minimises squared distance to cluster centres and is sensitive to scaling and its preferred cluster geometry.
concepts.example: Compare fitted centres for two blobs and for a curved two-moons dataset.

concepts.name: Initialisation and stability
concepts.explanation: Different starts can find different local solutions; inspect repeated runs and sensible n_init settings.
concepts.example: Fit several seeded runs and compare centre positions and objective values.

concepts.name: Density and noise
concepts.explanation: Density-based methods group connected dense regions and may label sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster.
concepts.example: Compare DBSCAN outputs under two eps values and report the number of noise points.

concepts.name: Silhouette limitations
concepts.explanation: An internal score evaluates a geometric criterion and can disagree with the business meaning of a grouping.
concepts.example: Compare silhouette scores and visual structure on synthetic curved groups before choosing a method.

concepts.name: PCA variance versus usefulness
concepts.explanation: PCA retains directions of high variance, which need not preserve the information relevant to a downstream target.
concepts.example: Create a noisy high-variance feature and a low-variance predictive feature and inspect what the first component preserves.

lessons.why: Explain every dimension and gradient in a small neural network.
lessons.summary: Explain every dimension and gradient in a small neural network.

concepts.name: Tensors
concepts.explanation: Tensors carry data, dtype and device; shape errors can survive broadcasting and corrupt training.
concepts.example: A linear layer maps a (batch, features) tensor to (batch, outputs).

concepts.name: Forward pass
concepts.explanation: Layers compose parameterized transformations to produce predictions.
concepts.example: A two-layer MLP applies linear, ReLU and linear operations.

concepts.name: Backpropagation and autograd
concepts.explanation: Reverse-mode differentiation accumulates gradients through a computation graph; gradients must be cleared between updates.
concepts.example: Call optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward() and optimizer.step() in order.

lessons.title: Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, GELU and softmax
lessons.why: Choose nonlinearities and interpret multiclass outputs correctly.
lessons.summary: Choose nonlinearities and interpret multiclass outputs correctly.

concepts.name: Hidden activations
concepts.explanation: Sigmoid/tanh can saturate; ReLU gates negative values; GELU smoothly weights inputs and is common in transformers.
concepts.example: Plot values and derivatives for these activations.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.explanation: Softmax exponentiates and normalizes logits into probabilities; subtracting the maximum improves numerical stability.
