concepts.name: Matrix multiplication versus elementwise multiplication
concepts.explanation: The @ operator contracts an inner dimension, while * multiplies matching or broadcast elements.

concepts.name: Views, reshape and contiguity
concepts.explanation: A view shares storage and some views require compatible strides; reshape may allocate a copy.

concepts.explanation: A parameter influences a loss through many intermediate values; reverse-mode differentiation sums contributions from every path.

concepts.name: Leaf tensors and gradient accumulation

concepts.name: Detach and no_grad
concepts.explanation: detach breaks graph connectivity and no_grad avoids building a graph; neither is a substitute for switching dropout to evaluation mode.
concepts.example: Detach a hidden state intentionally, then explain why detaching the final loss prevents training.

concepts.name: Finite-difference gradient checks
concepts.explanation: A central difference estimates a derivative from nearby loss values; use double precision and avoid nondifferentiable points.

concepts.explanation: Repeated multiplication through depth can shrink or enlarge gradients; inspect norms instead of guessing from the loss alone.

concepts.name: Reduction and masked losses

concepts.example: Mask padded token positions and compare sums and means across batches with different valid-token counts.

concepts.name: Channels and parameter sharing
concepts.explanation: Each output channel learns a kernel across its input channels and reuses that kernel at spatial positions.

concepts.explanation: Stacking layers changes the input region that can influence one output; stride and dilation alter that growth.
concepts.example: Compare two stride-one 3x3 layers with one 5x5 layer for receptive-field size and parameter count.

concepts.name: Pooling and spatial information
concepts.explanation: Max or average pooling aggregates local values and reduces resolution; fine position information may be lost.
concepts.example: Apply 2x2 max pooling to a hand-written 4x4 matrix and trace which values survive.

concepts.name: Grouped and depthwise convolution
concepts.explanation: Groups restrict which input channels connect to an output group; depthwise convolution processes channels separately before optional mixing.
concepts.example: Compare parameter counts for a standard convolution and depthwise-plus-pointwise layers.

lessons.title: Classification, detection and segmentation
lessons.why: Choose outputs and evaluation criteria that match the visual question instead of treating all image tasks as classification.
lessons.summary: Choose outputs and evaluation criteria that match the visual question instead of treating all image tasks as classification.

concepts.name: Classification outputs
concepts.explanation: An image classifier predicts a class distribution for a whole image and does not directly identify object locations.
concepts.example: Classify generated images containing either a vertical or horizontal bar.

concepts.name: Detection boxes
concepts.explanation: An object detector predicts a variable set of classes, boxes and scores; box coordinate conventions must be explicit.
concepts.example: Convert a box from x,y,width,height to x1,y1,x2,y2 and reject negative dimensions.

concepts.name: Segmentation masks
concepts.explanation: Semantic segmentation assigns a class to each pixel, while instance segmentation distinguishes separate objects of a class.
concepts.example: Generate a 16x16 square mask and compare a pixel classifier with a whole-image label.

concepts.name: Intersection over union
concepts.explanation: IoU measures overlap divided by union for boxes or masks and is different from classification accuracy.
concepts.example: Compute IoU for identical, disjoint and partially overlapping rectangles.

concepts.name: Task-specific errors
concepts.explanation: Missed objects, duplicate detections and incorrect boundaries require different error analysis than a wrong image class.
concepts.example: Create an error table separating missed rectangles from incorrect mask boundaries.

exercise.title: Lab: Classification, detection and segmentation
exercise.brief: Generate tiny images with rectangular objects and annotations. Implement box conversion, IoU and a threshold-based segmentation baseline on CPU; report classification and localisation errors separately.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Generate tiny images with rectangular objects and annotations. Implement box conversion, IoU and a threshold-based segmentation baseline on CPU; report classification and localisation errors separately.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Transfer learning, augmentation and frozen backbones
lessons.why: Reuse visual representations without leaking evaluation data or assuming all layers should be fine-tuned.
lessons.summary: Reuse visual representations without leaking evaluation data or assuming all layers should be fine-tuned.

concepts.name: Label-preserving augmentation
concepts.explanation: A transform is useful only when it preserves the target meaning for the intended task.
concepts.example: A horizontal flip may preserve a cat class but invert left/right labels in a navigation dataset.

concepts.name: Frozen features versus fine-tuning
concepts.explanation: A frozen backbone learns only a new head; fine-tuning updates selected pretrained layers and can overfit small data.
concepts.example: Freeze a tiny feature extractor and assert that its weights do not change after one training step.

concepts.name: Input preprocessing contracts
concepts.explanation: Pretrained weights assume particular ranges, channels and normalisation; mismatches can damage inference.
concepts.example: Write one preprocessing function shared by the training evaluation path and the API.

concepts.name: Discriminative learning rates
concepts.explanation: Different parameter groups can use smaller updates for pretrained layers and larger updates for a new head.
concepts.example: Create two optimiser groups and log their rates before the first update.

concepts.name: Train-only randomness
concepts.explanation: Random augmentations belong on training data; evaluation uses a documented deterministic transform.
concepts.example: Call evaluation preprocessing twice and assert identical outputs for the same generated image.

exercise.title: Lab: Transfer learning, augmentation and frozen backbones
exercise.brief: Train a tiny feature extractor on generated image shapes, transfer it to a related shape task and compare frozen versus unfrozen training on CPU. Include a shared preprocessing contract and a test that frozen parameters stay fixed.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Train a tiny feature extractor on generated image shapes, transfer it to a related shape task and compare frozen versus unfrozen training on CPU. Include a shared preprocessing contract and a test that frozen parameters stay fixed.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU and teacher forcing
lessons.why: Understand sequence state and training/inference differences before using a sequence model.
lessons.summary: Understand sequence state and training/inference differences before using a sequence model.

concepts.name: Hidden-state recurrence
concepts.explanation: An RNN repeatedly transforms the current input and previous state; the state summarises a sequence prefix.
concepts.example: Trace a two-step scalar recurrence by hand before running a batched RNN.

concepts.name: LSTM and GRU gates
concepts.explanation: Gates regulate what information is retained and updated; LSTM has a separate cell state while GRU uses a different state update.
concepts.example: Draw the shapes of LSTM hidden and cell states for two layers and a batch of four.

concepts.name: Teacher forcing
concepts.explanation: A decoder may receive the true preceding token during training but its own output during generation, creating a mismatch.
concepts.example: Compare next-token prediction when the previous symbol is correct versus deliberately corrupted.

concepts.name: Truncated backpropagation through time
concepts.explanation: Breaking a long sequence into segments controls memory by detaching state at chosen boundaries.
concepts.example: Carry a hidden state across three chunks and detach it between optimiser updates.

concepts.name: Sequence leakage and splits
concepts.explanation: Overlapping windows from the same underlying series can leak nearly identical information across splits.
concepts.example: Split a generated series by time before constructing training and validation windows.

exercise.title: Lab: RNN, LSTM, GRU and teacher forcing
exercise.brief: Train a tiny recurrent predictor on a generated repeating integer sequence on CPU. Compare teacher-forced accuracy with free-running generation and show that a time-based split precedes window creation.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Train a tiny recurrent predictor on a generated repeating integer sequence on CPU. Compare teacher-forced accuracy with free-running generation and show that a time-based split precedes window creation.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Queries, keys, values, masks and multi-head attention
lessons.why: Trace attention calculations and masking explicitly instead of treating a transformer layer as a black box.
lessons.summary: Trace attention calculations and masking explicitly instead of treating a transformer layer as a black box.

concepts.name: Queries, keys and values
concepts.explanation: Learned projections create vectors used to match positions and aggregate information; Q and K determine weights applied to V.
concepts.example: For a three-token sequence, write the Q, K and V shapes and the resulting 3x3 score matrix.

concepts.name: Scaled dot-product scores
concepts.explanation: Attention weights are softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k)) along the key dimension; scaling moderates score magnitudes.
concepts.example: Compute two attention scores by hand and verify each query row sums to one after softmax.

concepts.name: Causal and padding masks
concepts.explanation: A causal mask hides future positions and a padding mask hides non-data positions; APIs can differ in boolean-mask conventions.
concepts.example: Alter a future token and assert that an earlier token output does not change in a causal layer.

concepts.name: Multi-head projections
concepts.explanation: Heads learn different subspace attention patterns, then concatenate and project their outputs.
concepts.example: Split D=16 into four heads of size four and assert each reshape and transpose.

concepts.name: Quadratic attention cost
concepts.explanation: A dense attention score matrix grows with sequence length squared, even though implementations may reduce stored intermediates.
concepts.example: Compare the score-matrix element count for 64 versus 128 tokens before allocating a large example.

exercise.title: Lab: Queries, keys, values, masks and multi-head attention
exercise.brief: Implement a one-head causal attention layer for four toy tokens using CPU tensors. Compare with the library operation, verify row sums and mask behaviour, then extend it to two heads with shape assertions.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Implement a one-head causal attention layer for four toy tokens using CPU tensors. Compare with the library operation, verify row sums and mask behaviour, then extend it to two heads with shape assertions.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Transformer blocks, positions and encoder/decoder tasks
lessons.why: Connect transformer internals to the model interfaces used in embedding, classification and text generation.
lessons.summary: Connect transformer internals to the model interfaces used in embedding, classification and text generation.

concepts.name: Residual and feed-forward sublayers
concepts.explanation: A transformer block combines attention, residual paths, normalisation and a position-wise feed-forward network.
concepts.example: Print the shape after every sublayer of a tiny block and verify the residual addition dimensions.

concepts.name: Position information
concepts.explanation: Attention alone does not encode token order; absolute or relative positional mechanisms provide order information.
concepts.example: Compare token embeddings before and after adding sinusoidal positions to the same permuted sequence.

concepts.name: Encoder, decoder and cross-attention
concepts.explanation: Encoders commonly use bidirectional context; causal decoders predict continuations; cross-attention reads a separate source representation.
concepts.example: Sketch masks for sentence embedding, autoregressive generation and sequence-to-sequence translation.

concepts.name: Next-token label shifting
concepts.explanation: A language model predicts the next token from preceding tokens, so inputs and targets are offset by one position.
concepts.example: For [A,B,C,D], train inputs [A,B,C] against targets [B,C,D].

concepts.name: Pre-norm versus post-norm
concepts.explanation: The position of normalisation relative to residual addition affects the block computation and training behaviour.
concepts.example: Implement both block orders with identical shapes and document the actual equations used.

exercise.title: Lab: Transformer blocks, positions and encoder/decoder tasks
exercise.brief: Build a two-block character transformer with D=16 and a context of eight tokens on CPU. Demonstrate label shifting, causal masks and generation, and compare its held-out loss with a bigram baseline.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Build a two-block character transformer with D=16 and a context of eight tokens on CPU. Demonstrate label shifting, causal masks and generation, and compare its held-out loss with a bigram baseline.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Causal convolutions, dilation and hierarchical sequence models
lessons.why: Compare recurrent, convolutional and attention-based sequence processing using explicit context boundaries.
lessons.summary: Compare recurrent, convolutional and attention-based sequence processing using explicit context boundaries.

concepts.name: One-dimensional channel layout
concepts.explanation: Conv1d commonly uses batch, channels, length, whereas token embeddings are often stored as batch, length, features.
concepts.example: Transpose a B,T,D embedding tensor to B,D,T before a sequence convolution.

concepts.name: Causal padding
concepts.explanation: A causal convolution must not read a future position; ordinary symmetric padding can leak later tokens.
concepts.example: Left-pad a toy sequence and assert that changing its final value leaves earlier outputs unchanged.

concepts.name: Dilation
concepts.explanation: Dilated kernels space their input positions apart, expanding the receptive field without increasing kernel element count.
concepts.example: Trace which input indices influence one output for kernel size three and dilation two.

concepts.name: Hierarchical context aggregation
concepts.explanation: Stacking local transformations combines longer context while preserving explicit shape and ordering contracts.
concepts.example: Build a two-level character-context aggregator and show which characters influence a prediction.

concepts.name: Architecture comparison
concepts.explanation: Recurrent, convolutional and attention models differ in state, receptive field and computation; compare them on one fixed task.
concepts.example: Compare a tiny recurrent predictor and a causal Conv1d predictor using the same synthetic sequence split.

exercise.title: Lab: Causal convolutions, dilation and hierarchical sequence models
exercise.brief: Build a CPU causal Conv1d predictor for a generated character sequence. Test future-token isolation, calculate its receptive field and compare with a bigram baseline; treat the WaveNet video as the hierarchical-model foundation, not a full dilated-convolution implementation.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Build a CPU causal Conv1d predictor for a generated character sequence. Test future-token isolation, calculate its receptive field and compare with a bigram baseline; treat the WaveNet video as the hierarchical-model foundation, not a full dilated-convolution implementation.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Embeddings, contrastive learning and metric losses
lessons.why: Learn why an embedding space must match the downstream similarity task and evaluation setup.
lessons.summary: Learn why an embedding space must match the downstream similarity task and evaluation setup.

concepts.name: Learned embedding tables
concepts.explanation: An embedding lookup selects trainable rows rather than computing a meaningful representation from the integer ID itself.
concepts.example: Train a tiny token table and show that renumbering tokens consistently does not change the task.

concepts.name: Cosine and Euclidean distance
concepts.explanation: Distance choices interact with vector norms; normalised vectors make cosine and dot-product rankings agree.
concepts.example: Compare the nearest neighbours before and after normalising synthetic vectors with different magnitudes.

concepts.name: Positive and negative pairs
concepts.explanation: Contrastive training requires a meaningful rule for related and unrelated examples; false negatives can damage learning.
concepts.example: Construct two augmented views of one generated shape as a positive pair and document possible false negatives.

concepts.name: Triplet margin
concepts.explanation: A triplet loss penalises an anchor whose positive is not closer than its negative by a chosen margin.
concepts.example: Compute max(0, d(a,p)-d(a,n)+margin) for three two-dimensional points.

concepts.name: Retrieval evaluation
concepts.explanation: Evaluate neighbours against held-out relevance labels instead of trusting an attractive two-dimensional plot.
concepts.example: Measure recall@3 on a small labelled vector set and inspect failures from hard negatives.

exercise.title: Lab: Embeddings, contrastive learning and metric losses
exercise.brief: Train a tiny two-dimensional embedding on generated labelled points with triplet loss. Keep train and evaluation point IDs separate, compare cosine and Euclidean retrieval, and report recall@3 with hard-negative errors.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Train a tiny two-dimensional embedding on generated labelled points with triplet loss. Keep train and evaluation point IDs separate, compare cosine and Euclidean retrieval, and report recall@3 with hard-negative errors.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Autoencoders, latent spaces and variational objectives
lessons.why: Distinguish reconstruction from probabilistic generation before choosing an anomaly or generation method.
lessons.summary: Distinguish reconstruction from probabilistic generation before choosing an anomaly or generation method.

concepts.name: Encoder and decoder bottlenecks
concepts.explanation: An autoencoder compresses and reconstructs inputs; a useful bottleneck restricts what can be copied.
concepts.example: Train a 20-to-2-to-20 network on generated vectors and inspect reconstruction error.

concepts.name: Denoising reconstruction
concepts.explanation: A denoising model receives corrupted inputs and learns a clean target; corruption must resemble the intended use case.
concepts.example: Add Gaussian noise to generated waveforms and reconstruct the clean signal.

concepts.name: Variational latent distributions
concepts.explanation: A VAE encoder parameterises a distribution instead of one fixed code, enabling a regularised latent-space objective.
concepts.example: Produce a mean and log variance for each latent dimension and inspect their shapes.

concepts.name: Reparameterisation trick
concepts.explanation: A Gaussian latent sample can be written as mean+standard_deviation*epsilon so gradients reach the distribution parameters.
concepts.example: Use fixed sampled epsilon to check gradients through a two-dimensional latent sample.

concepts.name: Reconstruction plus KL terms
concepts.explanation: The VAE objective balances data reconstruction with divergence from a prior; loss reduction and scaling affect that balance.
concepts.example: Log reconstruction and KL components separately rather than comparing only their total.

exercise.title: Lab: Autoencoders, latent spaces and variational objectives
exercise.brief: Build a tiny CPU denoising autoencoder for generated sine waves. Add a two-dimensional variational bottleneck, plot reconstruction and KL terms separately, and describe why reconstruction error alone does not prove anomaly-detection quality.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Build a tiny CPU denoising autoencoder for generated sine waves. Add a two-dimensional variational bottleneck, plot reconstruction and KL terms separately, and describe why reconstruction error alone does not prove anomaly-detection quality.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: GAN and diffusion mechanics on toy distributions
lessons.why: Compare adversarial and denoising generation objectives without needing large image models or paid compute.
lessons.summary: Compare adversarial and denoising generation objectives without needing large image models or paid compute.

concepts.name: Adversarial objectives
concepts.explanation: A generator and discriminator optimise different objectives in an interacting process; improving one loss does not guarantee better samples.
concepts.example: Fit a generator to points from two Gaussian clusters and inspect whether both clusters appear.

concepts.name: Alternating updates and detach
concepts.explanation: Discriminator training uses generated examples without updating the generator; generator training must preserve its gradient path.
concepts.example: Check parameter changes after each half-step and catch an accidental generator detach during its own update.

concepts.name: Mode collapse
concepts.explanation: A generator can produce only a subset of the data distribution while fooling a limited discriminator.
concepts.example: Measure coverage of both toy clusters rather than showing only a few appealing samples.

concepts.name: Forward noise and reverse denoising
concepts.explanation: A diffusion setup progressively adds noise and learns a reverse denoising process conditioned on noise level.
concepts.example: Plot a two-dimensional point distribution after several increasing noise levels.

concepts.name: Sampling steps and evaluation
concepts.explanation: A learned denoiser must be paired with a specified sampling procedure; more steps change runtime and may change quality.
concepts.example: Compare a few denoising steps on generated points and report coverage and runtime without extrapolating to image quality.

exercise.title: Lab: GAN and diffusion mechanics on toy distributions
exercise.brief: On CPU, simulate forward diffusion on two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and fit a small noise-prediction MLP. Implement a minimal documented sampler; compare its outputs with a tiny GAN or a recorded GAN failure example.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: On CPU, simulate forward diffusion on two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and fit a small noise-prediction MLP. Implement a minimal documented sampler; compare its outputs with a tiny GAN or a recorded GAN failure example.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Overfit one batch, diagnose loss and debug numerical failures
lessons.why: Locate implementation problems before spending time on bigger models or long training runs.
lessons.summary: Locate implementation problems before spending time on bigger models or long training runs.

concepts.name: Overfit a tiny batch
concepts.explanation: A sufficiently flexible model should reduce the loss of a small consistent training set; failure often signals a pipeline or optimisation bug.
concepts.example: Disable regularisation and fit eight generated labelled examples before training on a larger dataset.

concepts.name: Loss baselines
concepts.explanation: Compare the initial objective to a simple expected baseline rather than assuming any decreasing number is good.
concepts.example: For a balanced K-class task, compare initial cross-entropy with log(K).

concepts.name: Gradient and update checks
concepts.explanation: A nonzero loss is not enough: parameters must receive finite gradients and actual updates.
concepts.example: Record grad norm and parameter delta before and after one optimiser step.

concepts.name: Numerical non-finites
concepts.explanation: NaN and infinity can enter through invalid operations, unstable exponentials or exploding updates; find the first failing tensor.
concepts.example: Inject log(0) into a toy graph and use finite checks to locate its origin.

concepts.name: Train/validation curves and errors
concepts.explanation: Learning curves suggest hypotheses about underfitting, overfitting or shift, but require examples and controlled experiments to confirm.
concepts.example: Compare a wrong-label dataset with a leaky split and explain why their curves can mislead.

exercise.title: Lab: Overfit one batch, diagnose loss and debug numerical failures
exercise.brief: Create three deliberately broken CPU training runs: detached output, mismatched targets and excessive learning rate. Write a diagnostic checklist, show the first failing assertion and demonstrate each corrected run.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Create three deliberately broken CPU training runs: detached output, mismatched targets and excessive learning rate. Write a diagnostic checklist, show the first failing assertion and demonstrate each corrected run.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Profiling, batching, precision and portable model artifacts
lessons.why: Measure the actual serving bottleneck and package the preprocessing and model state needed to reproduce predictions.
lessons.summary: Measure the actual serving bottleneck and package the preprocessing and model state needed to reproduce predictions.

concepts.name: Warmup and measurement boundaries
concepts.explanation: Initial setup and caching can distort timings; define whether a measurement includes preprocessing and queueing.
concepts.example: Warm up a tiny CPU model, then time preprocessing, inference and total request work separately.

concepts.name: Batch throughput versus latency
concepts.explanation: Batching amortises overhead but waiting to fill a batch can increase individual request latency.
concepts.example: Compare batch sizes one, eight and sixteen on the same 128 generated examples.

concepts.name: Precision and hardware support
concepts.explanation: Reduced precision is useful only where supported and accurate enough; CPU execution does not require a GPU mixed-precision lab.
concepts.example: Keep the required baseline in float32 and inspect alternative dtype support before testing it.

concepts.name: Checkpoint contracts
concepts.explanation: Weights alone do not describe architecture, preprocessing, label order or training provenance.
concepts.example: Save state_dict with a versioned configuration, normalisation constants and a label map.

concepts.name: Prediction parity
concepts.explanation: An exported or reloaded artifact must produce sufficiently similar outputs on fixed representative fixtures.
concepts.example: Compare logits before and after a save/load round trip using an explicit numerical tolerance.

exercise.title: Lab: Profiling, batching, precision and portable model artifacts
exercise.brief: Profile a small CPU network with three batch sizes, save weights plus metadata, reload in a fresh process and assert prediction parity. Report latency and throughput separately and document unsupported hardware-specific optimisations.
deliverables: Runnable code or notebook with a small reproducible input
README explaining decisions, results and limitations
acceptance: Profile a small CPU network with three batch sizes, save weights plus metadata, reload in a fresh process and assert prediction parity. Report latency and throughput separately and document unsupported hardware-specific optimisations.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Audio sampling, spectrograms and multimodal fusion
lessons.why: Understand how non-text signals become model inputs and evaluate alignment before combining modalities.
lessons.summary: Understand how non-text signals become model inputs and evaluate alignment before combining modalities.

concepts.name: Sampling rate and duration
concepts.explanation: The number of audio samples depends on duration and sampling rate; changing metadata without resampling changes interpretation.
concepts.example: Generate one second of a 440Hz sine wave at 16kHz and verify it contains 16000 samples.

concepts.name: Windows and spectrograms
concepts.explanation: A short-time Fourier transform computes local frequency content using a window and hop length; a spectrogram trades time and frequency resolution.
concepts.example: Compare two window sizes on generated tones and annotate the time/frequency axes.

concepts.name: Mel scaling and log values
concepts.explanation: Mel filterbanks group frequencies using a perceptual scale, and log energy needs a safe floor for silence.
concepts.example: Compute a mel spectrogram for a synthetic signal and verify a silent input produces finite log values.

concepts.name: Early versus late fusion
concepts.explanation: Modalities can be combined at feature level or after separate predictions, but their sample identity and timing must agree.
concepts.example: Join a tiny audio-feature table with text labels by a stable sample ID and detect one mismatched pair.

concepts.name: Modality-specific evaluation
concepts.explanation: An overall multimodal score can hide dependence on one modality or failure on missing inputs.
concepts.example: Compare both-input, audio-only, text-only and missing-audio conditions using deterministic toy predictors.

Fuse them with synthetic text labels by sample ID, detect a deliberate alignment error and evaluate missing-modality behaviour. The linked videos cover sequence/vision foundations; audio-specific preprocessing is in the written course.

Fuse them with synthetic text labels by sample ID, detect a deliberate alignment error and evaluate missing-modality behaviour. The linked videos cover sequence/vision foundations; audio-specific preprocessing is in the written course.
Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

lessons.title: Rewards, policies, value estimates and exploration
lessons.why: Distinguish reward-based decision learning from ordinary tool orchestration before choosing a reinforcement-learning approach.
lessons.summary: Distinguish reward-based decision learning from ordinary tool orchestration before choosing a reinforcement-learning approach.

concepts.name: States, actions and transitions
concepts.explanation: A sequential decision problem specifies what is observed, which actions are allowed and how the environment changes.
concepts.example: Define a three-state toy environment with two actions and explicit terminal transitions.

concepts.name: Reward and return
concepts.explanation: Immediate rewards differ from discounted future return, and reward design determines what behaviour is incentivised.
concepts.example: Calculate the discounted sum for a short reward sequence at two discount factors.

concepts.name: Policy versus value
concepts.explanation: A policy chooses actions while a value estimate predicts expected return under specified assumptions.
concepts.example: Represent an epsilon-greedy bandit policy separately from its action-value estimates.

concepts.name: Exploration versus exploitation
concepts.explanation: Learning about uncertain actions can improve future choices while lowering immediate reward.
concepts.example: Compare always taking the first apparently good action with seeded epsilon-greedy exploration on a two-arm bandit.

concepts.name: Evaluation and reward hacking
concepts.explanation: A higher training reward may reflect exploiting the reward definition rather than meeting the real user goal.
concepts.example: Add a misleading reward bonus in a toy environment and show why an independent success measure is needed.

exercise.title: Lab: Rewards, policies, value estimates and exploration
exercise.brief: Implement a seeded two-arm bandit simulation entirely on CPU. Compare greedy and epsilon-greedy policies over repeated runs, plot average reward/regret and document why a tool-calling application does not automatically need reinforcement learning.

README explaining decisions, results and limitations

Include at least one happy-path and one failure/edge-case check; explain the output using the concept checklist.

concepts.name: Embeddings and transformers

concepts.example: Reserve output space before adding retrieved chunks.

concepts.name: Model selection
concepts.explanation: Task quality, latency, context size, license and hardware matter more than one leaderboard.
concepts.example: Score candidate models against a fixed ten-question evaluation set.

concepts.name: Open and closed models
concepts.explanation: Available weights permit local serving, but licenses and hardware still constrain usage.
concepts.example: Record a model license and intended use before distributing it.

concepts.name: Self-hosting
concepts.explanation: Local serving needs memory budgets and operational checks; mock inference is a valid development fallback.
concepts.example: Use a recorded-response fixture when a laptop cannot run the selected model.

concepts.name: Stop conditions

concepts.name: Quantisation tradeoffs
concepts.explanation: Reduced-bit weights may lower memory use but require compatible kernels and quality checks; they do not automatically reduce every runtime cost.
concepts.example: Compare stored sizes and reconstruction errors for a tiny weight vector quantised to a small integer range.

concepts.name: Caching boundaries and privacy

concepts.explanation: A queue can deliver a job more than once, so receiving a message does not prove its side effect has not already happened.
concepts.example: Process the same ingestion ID twice and assert one logical document version is created.

concepts.name: Exponential backoff and jitter
concepts.explanation: Retries should be spaced and randomised to avoid synchronised retry bursts, with a cap and attempt budget.
concepts.example: Compute retry delays for five fake failures using a seeded random source.

concepts.name: Transient versus permanent errors
concepts.explanation: A temporary timeout may warrant retry while an invalid input usually needs correction rather than repeated execution.
concepts.example: Retry a fake network timeout but send a malformed-document job directly to a terminal failure state.

concepts.name: Deduplication transaction
concepts.explanation: Deduplication and the protected state change must be coordinated to avoid a crash between effect and acknowledgement.
concepts.example: Simulate a crash after a write but before acknowledgement and verify replay remains safe.

concepts.name: Backpressure and capacity
concepts.explanation: A bounded queue and explicit rejection or waiting policy prevent overload from consuming all memory.
concepts.example: Submit more jobs than a toy queue can hold and verify the chosen full-queue behaviour.
